questions.question: For `x <- c(5, NA, 8, 2)`, the call `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` returns `5`, but the next line `sd(x)` returns `NA`. Why does `sd(x)` give `NA`?
options: `sd()` skips gaps with `use = "complete.obs"`, as `cor()` does, not with `na.rm`.
`na.rm = TRUE` applied only to that `mean()` call; `x` itself still contains the `NA`.
With one entry missing the spread is undefined, so `sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)` is `NA` as well.
`sd()` cannot skip gaps at all, so it returns `NA` for every vector that contains one.

questions.question: For `x <- c(4, NA, 7)`, R prints `[1] NA NA NA` for `x == NA`. Why does this comparison not locate the missing second entry?
options: R compares `x` with the text `"NA"`, and none of the three entries equals that text.
`NA` has length 0, so it cannot be recycled to the three positions of `x`.
`==` cannot compare a number with a logical value, so R gives up in every position.
Each comparison asks if a value equals an unknown value, so each answer is unknown.

questions.question: For `x <- c(8, 3, NA, 5, NA)`, what does R print for `which(is.na(x))`?
For `x <- c(7, NA, 3, NA, NA, 1, 9)`, what does R print for `sum(is.na(x))`?
A character vector of survey answers is `v <- c("NA", NA, "n/a")`. What does R print for `is.na(v)`?
A numeric vector `x` holds 500 recorded incomes and may contain gaps. Which call returns a single `TRUE` or `FALSE` saying whether `x` has at least one missing entry?
For `x <- c(2, NA, 8, NA, 1)`, what does R print for `x[!is.na(x)]`?
For `a <- c(1, NA, 3, 4)` and `b <- c(10, 20, NA, 40)`, what does R print for `a + b`?
For `df <- data.frame(a = c(1, NA, 3, 4, 5), b = c(2, NA, 6, NA, 1))`, what does R print for `nrow(df[complete.cases(df), ])`?
For `df <- data.frame(name = c("Ann", "Bob", "Cat", "Dan"), sen = c(2, NA, 5, NA))`, what does R print for `df[is.na(df[["sen"]]), "name"]`?

Vectors `age` and `pay` hold the age and pay of the same 8 workers, position by position; only `age[3]` and `pay[6]` are `NA`. A student runs `cor(age[!is.na(age)], pay[!is.na(pay)])`. What goes wrong?
options: R returns a number, but several ages are now paired with other workers' pay.
Nothing: it equals `cor(age, pay, use = "complete.obs")`, which drops the same two gaps.
R stops with an error, because the two cleaned vectors no longer have the same length.
R returns `NA`, because `cor()` needs `use = "complete.obs"` even after the gaps are removed.

questions.question: A data frame `df` has columns `Age`, `Dept`, `Seniority` and `Comment`, with gaps in all four. An analysis uses only `Dept` and `Seniority`. How does `df[!is.na(df[["Dept"]]) & !is.na(df[["Seniority"]]), ]` compare with `df[complete.cases(df), ]`?
options: They always keep the same rows, because both remove every row that has a gap.
`complete.cases()` keeps more rows, since it drops a row only if all its columns are missing.
The first keeps every row the second keeps, and rows missing only `Age` or `Comment`.
The second keeps more rows, since `complete.cases()` ignores gaps in character columns.

questions.question: For the numeric vector `x <- c(2, NA, 5)`, what does R print for `x == "NA"`?
The paired vectors `x <- c(2, NA, 5, 1, 7, 4)` and `y <- c(3, 6, 8, NA, 9, 5)` hold two variables for the same six workers. Which call returns the same value as `cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs")`?
The bonuses of the three workers in one team were all unrecorded, so `b <- c(NA, NA, NA)`. What does R print for `mean(b, na.rm = TRUE)`?
For `df <- data.frame(a = c(1, NA, 3, NA, 5), b = c(2, 4, NA, NA, 6))`, a student sets `keep <- !is.na(df[["a"]]) | !is.na(df[["b"]])`. What does R print for `nrow(df[keep, ])`?

In a survey, 40 of 200 workers did not report their bonus, so the vector `bonus` has 40 `NA` entries. Workers with low bonuses were much less likely to report. What does `mean(bonus, na.rm = TRUE)` give?
options: The average bonus of all 200 workers, because `na.rm = TRUE` corrects for the gaps.
An average that is too low, because the 40 gaps enter the sum as zeros.
Close to the average of all 200, only based on fewer values, as for any 160 of them.
The average of the 160 reported bonuses, which is likely above that of all 200.

The vector `x <- c(0/0, 4, NA, 1, 0/0, NA, NA)` mixes undefined results of $0/0$ with unrecorded values. Which call counts only the unrecorded values, the `NA` entries?
For `df <- data.frame(x = c(2, NA, 6, 4), y = c(1, 3, NA, 5))`, a student runs `clean <- df[complete.cases(df), ]`. What does R print for `c(mean(df[["x"]], na.rm = TRUE), mean(clean[["x"]]))`?
